NoteNlpAccessor::normalize_numbers¶

Back to Note NLP Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note NoteNlpAccessor::normalize_numbers() const

Replace Each Numeric Run With A Canonical Zero¶

normalize_numbers() replaces every run beginning with an ASCII digit by the single character 0. It preserves the surrounding sentence while making surface forms such as 7, 1,234.50, and 2024-01-02 compare as the same numeric category. Use it when downstream logic needs ordinary text containing a compact canonical value. Use mask_numbers() instead when an explicit [NUM] marker is important to readers or token classifiers.

A run follows this exact byte grammar:

Input byte

Effect inside a run

0 through 9

Always consumed.

, . - / : _ followed immediately by a digit

Separator and following numeric portion remain in the same run.

Any other byte

Ends the run and is preserved.

Therefore a date-shaped or time-shaped string is normalized as one run, even if it is not a valid calendar date or clock time. This method recognizes syntax, not numeric meaning. A leading sign is outside the run, so +7 becomes +0; digits embedded in an identifier are still found, so x8y becomes x0y; and 1..2 contains two runs because the first dot is not followed by a digit.

Only ASCII digits participate. The method does not parse values, round them, preserve magnitude, or distinguish dates, currency, versions, and identifiers. Apply a narrower semantic operation first when those distinctions matter.

The implementation scans each cell once and performs no regex compilation or backtracking. The result is a fresh Text Note with identical shape and cell order. It is idempotent because every replacement is itself one canonical numeric run. Empty and undefined behavior follows the other text transforms; non-Text dtypes are rejected.

Example 1: Several Numeric Surface Forms¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::note::make({"42 1,234.50 2024-01-02 +7 x8y"})
        .nlp().normalize_numbers()) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["0 0 0 +0 x0y"]

Example 2: Separator Boundaries¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::note::make({"1/2 3:45 6_000 1..2 and no digits"})
        .nlp().normalize_numbers()) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["0 0 0 0..0 and no digits"]

Example 3: Preserve Higher-Rank Structure¶

const auto matrix = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{" can't ", "12", "“yes”", "plain"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    matrix.nlp().normalize_numbers()) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  [" can't ", "0"], 
  ["“yes”", "plain"]
]

Example 4: Idempotence¶

const auto once = pluss::note::make({"Build 1847 costs $12.50"})
                      .nlp().normalize_numbers();
std::cout << "numbers idempotent=" << std::boolalpha
          << (once.nlp().normalize_numbers() == once).all().bool_item()
          << '\n';

Output¶

numbers idempotent=true

See Also¶

  • mask_numbers: use [NUM] rather than 0 while retaining the same run grammar.

  • mask_dates: recognize date-shaped spans with range checks.

  • mask_pii: apply semantic masking in precedence order.
